newsitem.title: ITALY: Mafia widow urges Mob molls to rise in revolt.
newsitem.headline: Mafia widow urges Mob molls to rise in revolt.

text.p: The widow of a Mafia boss has urged other mob women to "break their chains" and rebel against violence and crime after turning to God following the deaths of 21 relatives in a vendetta.
The dramatic appeal by Filippa Inzerillo, reported in Italian newspapers on Friday, cheered crime fighters and Church leaders who say women could unlock the secrets of Cosa Nostra.
"Women of the Mafia, rise in revolt," Inzerillo said.
"Break your chains and return to life."
She voiced forgiveness for jailed "boss of bosses" Salvatore "The Beast" Riina, whose rise to the top of the Mafia passed over the corpses of her husband, son and 19 other loved ones.
Guido Lo Forte, a leading investigator in the Sicilian capital Palermo, called Inzerillo's appeal an act of courage and conscience. "Finally, we have a piece of good news," he said.
"The women of the Mafia always know what their husbands, fathers or sons are up to," a female turncoat, Piera Aiello, was quoted by La Stampa newspaper as saying.
"If women decided to talk, Cosa Nostra would be beaten".
The mothers, wives and daughters of the Mafia have long held a subservient role in the crime organisation, bound by its deadly code of Omerta, or silence, but not admitted as members.
Recent evidence, however, suggests that many women are increasingly active in the Mafia itself, running Cosa Nostra's affairs while their menfolk languish behind bars.
Arrest figures show 89 women were accused of Mafia crimes last year compared with just one in 1989.
Inzerillo's husband Totuccio was gunned down in Sicily in May 1981 as Riina and his Corleonesi clan wiped out their rivals for control of the Mob.
The couple's son Giuseppe, 16, vowed revenge but was captured by the Corleonesi and never seen again.
Turncoats say one of Riina's most feared killers, the late Pino Greco, axed off Giuseppe's arm shouting "That way you won't shoot Riina" and finished him off with a bullet to the head.

"There are no beasts among men. Riina is a son of God who has erred. His spirit is sick and he should repent. I'm not saying he should go to the magistrates but he should talk to the Lord before it is too late," Filippa Inzerillo said.
Riina's wife, schoolteacher Antonietta Bagarella, has never spoken of her husband's affairs and remained out of sight with him during his 23 years on the run.
Bagarella's sister-in-law, Vincenzina Marchese, committed suicide after her brother broke with the Mob to turn state's evidence.

Inzerillo, whose blood ties to the Mafia stretch back generations and across the Atlantic to the Gambino clan in the United States, made her plea after undergoing a conversion to deep religious faith.
Newspapers said she had filled her home in Palermo with so many statues that it had become a virtual Roman Catholic shrine and that she had donated land to the Church.

"I don't know Signora Inzerillo but I believe that what she has said is very significant," Palermo's Archbishop Salvatore de Giorgi said. "I would like to hope that it is the sign...of an answer to our prayers".
